explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The commander hears a chained man ask politely for a word, and out comes "Do you speak Greek?" (Acts 21:37). I think he was surprised, because he had a different man in mind. Paul gets his turn to talk anyway.
Close to a family question, but that's not what the commander asks. He says, "Do you speak Greek?" (Acts 21:37). Paul's father never comes up in this exchange. Language is the question on the table.

Paul does bring up a teacher later in his speech, so I see why this one tempts. But the commander's first question is "Do you speak Greek?" (Acts 21:37). Paul's teacher doesn't come up until Acts 22:3.

explanations.answer: I am a Jew from Tarsus
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no ordinary city." (Acts 21:39). One sentence and he's clearly not the Egyptian rebel. Short, true and to the point.

explanations.answer: I am a Greek from Athens
explanations.explanation: The commander did just ask him about Greek, so I get the mix-up. But Paul says, "I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia…" (Acts 21:39). Athens never comes up in his answer.

explanations.answer: I am a trader from Alexandria
explanations.explanation: The commander did mention an Egyptian, so Alexandria is a fair guess. But Paul says, "I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia…" (Acts 21:39). He's no Egyptian and no trader in this answer.
Yep. Paul says, "Now I beg you to allow me to speak to the people." (Acts 21:39). A man in chains, asking for the mic. That's some nerve, and I mean it as a compliment.
Not this time, baker. Paul says, "Now I beg you to allow me to speak to the people." (Acts 21:39). He asks the commander for permission, and he gets it in verse 40. So it's True.
I get why you'd expect that, with a crowd this worked up. But the text says, "A great hush came over the crowd…" (Acts 21:40). So the shouting does not get louder. That makes it False.
Right, baker. Paul motions to the crowd, and the text says, "A great hush came over the crowd…" (Acts 21:40). That's quiet enough to hear a cookie crumble. A hush like that is worth noticing.

Yes, baker. Verse 40 says Paul "…addressed them in Hebrew…" (Acts 21:40). The commander had asked him, "Do you speak Greek?" (Acts 21:37), but the crowd heard Hebrew. Acts 22:2 says that when they heard him speak to them in Hebrew, they became even more quiet.
Latin is the Roman language, so I see the logic. But the text says Paul "…addressed them in Hebrew…" (Acts 21:40). Latin isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage.

Persian doesn't show up anywhere in this scene. Acts 21:40 says Paul "…addressed them in Hebrew…" The crowd heard it, and Acts 22:2 says they became even more quiet. Hebrew is the language of the speech.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "I was educated at the feet of Gamaliel in strict conformity to the law of our fathers." (Acts 22:3). He also says he was raised in this city, and then he names his teacher to the crowd. I bet that got their attention.
Nicodemus is a Pharisee who talks with Jesus at night (John 3:1-2). But he isn't the teacher Paul names. Paul says he was educated "…at the feet of Gamaliel…" (Acts 22:3).
Caiaphas was a high priest (Matthew 26:3), so I see why he comes to mind. But Paul names a different man. He says he was educated "…at the feet of Gamaliel…" (Acts 22:3).

Yes, baker. Paul says, "…suddenly a bright light from heaven flashed around me." (Acts 22:6). About noon, too, which is the brightest part of the day. A light that stands out at noon is not an ordinary light.

explanations.answer: A great wind from the sea
explanations.explanation: No wind is mentioned anywhere in Paul's account. He says, "…suddenly a bright light from heaven flashed around me." (Acts 22:6). Light is what he describes, not wind. A wind would be a very different scene.

explanations.answer: A pillar of fire from above
explanations.explanation: A pillar of fire is a big moment from Exodus (Exodus 13:21), so I see the pull. But Paul describes "…a bright light from heaven…" (Acts 22:6). He doesn't say fire.

That's the one, baker. Paul asked who was speaking, and Jesus answered, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting…" (Acts 22:8). Paul asked who it was and got a straight answer. I think that was a lot to take in on the ground.
Moses is a big name, so I see why he came to mind. But Jesus is the one who answers Paul, saying, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting…" (Acts 22:8). Paul was talking to Jesus Himself.
Gabriel is a name people know, so I see the pull. But it's Jesus who answers Paul, saying, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting…" (Acts 22:8). No angel is named in this scene.

Not quite, baker. Paul says, "My companions saw the light, but they could not understand the voice of the One speaking to me." (Acts 22:9). They saw the light, but they couldn't understand the voice. So this one is False.

Right. Paul says, "My companions saw the light, but they could not understand the voice of the One speaking to me." (Acts 22:9). They saw the light but could not understand the voice. I think that left them with a lot of questions.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "…my companions led me by the hand into Damascus." (Acts 22:11). The brilliance of the light had blinded him. The man who planned to march in with letters had to be walked in by the hand.

Not this time, baker. Paul says, "Because the brilliance of the light had blinded me, my companions led me by the hand into Damascus." (Acts 22:11). So it's True. A man who was on his way to apprehend people got led in by the hand.

Yes, baker. Ananias says, "Brother Saul," and then, "receive your sight." Paul says, "…at that moment I could see him." (Acts 22:13). The light had blinded him (Acts 22:11), and now he could see Ananias. I think being called brother was a kind way to start.

Paul heard the voice speaking to him (Acts 22:7), so hearing isn't what this verse turns on. What he needed was his sight, since the brilliance of the light had blinded him (Acts 22:11). Ananias says, "receive your sight." (Acts 22:13).

Paul spoke up when he asked, "Who are You, Lord?" (Acts 22:8), and again when he asked, "What should I do, Lord?" (Acts 22:10). So voice isn't what this verse is about. The light had blinded him (Acts 22:11), and Ananias says, "receive your sight." (Acts 22:13).
That's right, baker. Ananias says, "You will be His witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard." (Acts 22:15). A witness tells what he saw. And Paul had seen plenty.

Priest is a fair guess, and I see why it sounds right. But Ananias says, "You will be His witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard." (Acts 22:15). A witness tells what he has seen and heard. That's the job Paul is given.

Judge sounds like a big job, so I see the pull. But Ananias says, "You will be His witness to everyone of what you have seen and heard." (Acts 22:15). He wasn't told to sit in a seat. He was told to tell.

explanations.answer: Be baptized and wash his sins away
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Ananias says, "And now what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name." (Acts 22:16). Paul had just been led into Damascus blind (Acts 22:11), and now he's being told to get up. It sounds to me like a friend who has no time to waste.

explanations.answer: Go and report to the high priest
explanations.explanation: Paul was headed to Damascus with letters from the high priest and the Council (Acts 22:5), so I see why the high priest comes to mind. But Ananias says, "Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name." (Acts 22:16). That's a new road.

explanations.answer: Stay hidden until the danger passes
explanations.explanation: Hiding would be a sensible plan for a man in Paul's spot. But Ananias says, "Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name." (Acts 22:16). Nothing about hiding.

explanations.answer: The people won't accept his testimony
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The Lord says, "Hurry! Leave Jerusalem quickly, because the people here will not accept your testimony about Me." (Acts 22:18). Paul is telling this to the very crowd in Jerusalem. I think that makes this line hit hard.

explanations.answer: Ananias needs him back in Damascus
explanations.explanation: Ananias did help Paul in Damascus, so I see why this one comes to mind. But the Lord's reason is this: "…the people here will not accept your testimony about Me." (Acts 22:18). Ananias isn't mentioned in this vision.

explanations.answer: His work in Jerusalem is all done
explanations.explanation: That's a tidy reason, but it isn't the one the text gives. The Lord says, "…the people here will not accept your testimony about Me." (Acts 22:18). He doesn't say the work was finished.

explanations.answer: He watched over the garments of his killers
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "…I stood there giving my approval and watching over the garments of those who killed him." (Acts 22:20). He doesn't dress it up. He names exactly what he did, and that takes honesty.

explanations.answer: He tried to stop the crowd that killed him
explanations.explanation: That would be a different story, and Paul doesn't tell it. He says, "…I stood there giving my approval and watching over the garments of those who killed him." (Acts 22:20). He was there and he approved.

explanations.answer: He buried him outside the city walls
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say Paul buried anyone. He says, "…I stood there giving my approval and watching over the garments of those who killed him." (Acts 22:20). Watching over garments is what he did.

That's right, baker. The Lord says, "Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles." (Acts 22:21). Gentiles are people who aren't Jewish. The text says the crowd listened to Paul until this statement (Acts 22:22).
Samaritans are a fair guess, since they're another group people know. But the Lord says, "Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles." (Acts 22:21). Samaritans aren't named here.
The commander did bring up an Egyptian earlier, so I see the link. But the Lord says, "Go! I will send you far away to the Gentiles." (Acts 22:21). No single nation is named.

explanations.answer: That he is not fit to live
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, and it's a hard one. They shout, "Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live!" (Acts 22:22). I think this part hurts to read. Paul went from a hushed crowd to a roaring one in a single sentence.

explanations.answer: That he should be set free
explanations.explanation: I wish that were true, baker. But the crowd shouts, "Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live!" (Acts 22:22). They wanted him gone.

explanations.answer: That he should keep on speaking
explanations.explanation: They had been listening, so I see the logic. But once Paul says "Gentiles," they shout, "Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live!" (Acts 22:22). The listening ended right there.

explanations.answer: That Paul be flogged and questioned
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says the commander "…directed that Paul be flogged and interrogated…" (Acts 22:24). A flogging is a hard thing to read about, and I think it's heavy. Paul's about to say something that changes everything, though.

explanations.answer: That Paul be handed back to the crowd
explanations.explanation: The commander does the opposite. He ordered Paul brought into the barracks and "…directed that Paul be flogged and interrogated…" (Acts 22:24). Handing Paul back to the crowd isn't in that order.

explanations.answer: That Paul be locked up without food
explanations.explanation: Food is never mentioned here. The commander "…directed that Paul be flogged and interrogated…" (Acts 22:24). That's the order he gives.
Yes, baker. The commander wanted "…to determine the reason for this outcry against him." (Acts 22:24). He wanted to know why the crowd was shouting. His method was a hard one, though.
Not quite. The text says the commander wanted "…to determine the reason for this outcry against him." (Acts 22:24). So it's True. He wanted to know why they were yelling.

That's right, baker. Paul asks, "Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?" (Acts 22:25). He asks it while they're stretching him out to strap him down. Perfect timing for a question like that.
Soldier sounds close, since Paul is talking to a centurion (Acts 22:25). But Paul asks about flogging "…a Roman citizen without a trial?" (Acts 22:25). Citizen is the word.
That word doesn't show up in Paul's question. He asks, "Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?" (Acts 22:25). Citizen is what he says.
No, baker. The commander asks, "Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?" and Paul answers, "Yes," (Acts 22:27). He doesn't refuse. He answers the question straight, so it's False.

That's right. The commander asks, "Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?" and Paul answers, "Yes," (Acts 22:27). He answers plainly. Then the commander says he paid a high price for his own citizenship (Acts 22:28).
Yes, baker. Paul says, "But I was born a citizen…" (Acts 22:28). The commander paid a high price for his, and Paul's came with his birth. I think that's a mic drop, if I may.

explanations.answer: He paid an even higher price
explanations.explanation: That would be quite a bidding war. But Paul says, "But I was born a citizen…" (Acts 22:28). He didn't pay anything for it.
The text doesn't say that. Paul says, "But I was born a citizen…" (Acts 22:28). It came with his birth, not with his service.

Yes, baker. The text says "…the commander himself was alarmed when he realized that he had put a Roman citizen in chains." (Acts 22:29). He had chained a citizen. I bet that was a rough moment for him.

I don't think relief fits, and the text doesn't say it. It says the commander "…was alarmed when he realized that he had put a Roman citizen in chains." (Acts 22:29). He found out something he didn't know.
I doubt anybody in that room was laughing. The text says the commander "…was alarmed when he realized that he had put a Roman citizen in chains." (Acts 22:29). Alarmed is the word.
